concerns.text: The plan computes VIF for the full set of method dummy variables (PCA, t‑SNE, UMAP) while retaining an intercept. This creates perfect multicollinearity (the dummy‑variable trap), causing VIF to be infinite and the abort condition (VIF ≥ 5) to be triggered regardless of data quality. The analysis should drop one reference level or use effect coding before VIF calculation.

A Fixed‑Effects ANOVA (or Kruskal‑Wallis) is proposed on the outcome "fidelity" with predictor "method" but the design ignores the dataset factor. Since each method is applied to three distinct datasets, dataset‑to‑dataset variability is a confounder; the model should include a random intercept for dataset (mixed‑effects) or at least a fixed effect for dataset to avoid biased estimates of the method effect.

Only nine observations (3 datasets × 3 methods) will be available for the ANOVA/Kruskal‑Wallis test. This sample size is far below typical recommendations for reliable estimation of variance components and for assessing normality/homoscedasticity, making the statistical inference fragile.

The fidelity metrics (ARI and NMI) are bounded between 0 and 1. Applying a standard ANOVA assumes approximately normal, unbounded residuals with constant variance, which is unlikely for these bounded scores. A beta regression or appropriate transformation (e.g., logit) should be considered, or non‑parametric methods with permutation testing.

The sensitivity analysis sweeps Leiden resolution and reports variance of ARI/NMI across thresholds, then uses a fixed variance threshold (0.05) as a pass/fail criterion. This arbitrary cutoff is not justified statistically and may lead to binary decisions without proper uncertainty quantification.
